query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a CALPHAD‐based high-throughput design strategy will yield high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with improved phase stability, refined microstructure, and enhanced properties compared to those developed via traditional experimental methods.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or solidified HEA composition exhibiting a mix of phases and conventional microstructural inhomogeneity.
generation.intervention: Application of a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational screening and optimization process to select and tune alloy compositions using thermodynamic parameters.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled conditions (e.g., defined composition ranges and temperature profiles) with sufficient computational resources for parallel high-throughput calculations.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure with a dominant single-phase solid solution and reduced formation of undesired secondary or intermetallic phases.
generation.mechanism: By calculating key thermophysical parameters (e.g., mixing enthalpy, entropy, atomic size differences) via CALPHAD, the method rapidly screens compositions that favor phase stability and homogeneous microstructures, thus optimizing mechanical and physical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs developed through CALPHAD-based design will show a statistically significant improvement in phase purity, microstructure refinement, and mechanical performance (such as increased strength and ductility) relative to alloys produced by conventional trial-and-error approaches.
generation.baseline: HEAs designed without computational optimization which typically exhibit multiple phases, microstructural inhomogeneities, and suboptimal mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected for high-entropy alloy systems within the validated compositional and processing ranges; the approach may not directly translate to alloys with fundamentally different chemistries or processing routes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvements in phase stability and properties is uncertain until validated experimentally and may vary with the specific alloy system and processing parameters applied.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set developed using traditional alloy design methods and a second set designed using a CALPHAD-based high-throughput strategy. Process both sets under identical conditions and characterize the phase composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties.
measurements: Scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) for microstructural evaluation
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile strength, hardness, ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CALPHAD-designed HEAs do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in phase stability (e.g., a single-phase structure), microstructure refinement, and mechanical performance compared to the traditionally designed HEAs, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys.
